lines: Drum pattern generator driven by a phasor rather than a clock, a port of Mutable Instruments Grids: a ramp sweeps 32 steps of a bar, and three channels of triggers and accents come off a map
Selects the pattern source: Original and Henri are two maps of drum patterns, Euclid replaces them with a Euclidean rhythm on each channel
Moves east and west across the map of drum patterns, blending the four patterns nearest the point chosen; in Euclid it sets the pattern length for channel 1 instead
Moves north and south across the map of drum patterns, blending the four patterns nearest the point chosen; in Euclid it sets the pattern length for channel 2 instead
Adds random variation to the pattern, drawn afresh each time the phasor returns to 0V; at the bottom of its travel the bar repeats exactly. In Euclid it sets the pattern length for channel 3 instead
Sets how many of that channel's steps fire, from none at the bottom of its travel to the densest the chosen pattern offers at the top
A ramp from 0V to 10V across one bar, cut into 32 steps by where the voltage is; running it backwards plays the bar backwards, and holding the voltage steady holds one step
Added to the Mode knob at one mode per 2.5V, the total rounded and held within the three modes; it is read only while a cable is patched
Added to the Map X knob, 10V covering the knob's whole travel, and the total held within it
Added to the Map Y knob, 10V covering the knob's whole travel, and the total held within it
Added to the Chaos knob, 10V covering the knob's whole travel, and the total held within it
Added to that channel's Fill knob, 10V covering the knob's whole travel, and the total held within it
A 1ms pulse at 10V on each step that channel fires; the Trigger Mode menu item turns it into a gate lasting half a step instead
A 1ms pulse at 10V on the steps that channel fires with an accent; in Euclid it fires where that channel's Euclidean pattern comes back round to its start instead
Note — a phasor drives this, not a clock: a ramp rising from 0V to 10V once per bar, from Phasor Generator, Clock to Phasor or an LFO's saw output. Nothing moves here until one is patched in.
Note — in Euclid the patterns are read on every second step, so a bar holds 16 places rather than 32 and the odd-numbered steps are always silent.
Note — the lamp above each channel's jacks lights for 100ms whenever that channel fires, whichever of the two output jacks the pulse went to.
Note — every jack on the module is monophonic; only the first channel of a polyphonic cable is read, and each output carries one channel.
Menu — Trigger Mode: Pulse, Gate — Pulse sends a 1ms pulse on each hit, Gate holds the output high for the first half of the step the hit falls on

PhasorBeatMap.notes:
Read from the repository at commit 56bf82b, the tip of the default branch, whose plugin.json is byte-for-byte the installed one at version 2.0.0.

THIS MODULE IS NOT BUILT LIKE THE REST OF HETRICKCV. Every jack is read with getVoltage(), not getPolyVoltage, and the outputs are written to channel 0 alone, so the module is monophonic throughout. The phasor input also clamps to 0 to 10V (PhasorBeatMap.cpp:156) where the plugin's usual scaleAndWrapPhasor wraps; the sibling module PhasorWavetable in this same plugin does wrap. Neither difference is documented anywhere.

The phasor input is given no family, following the finished HetrickCV entry, where phasor jacks carry none either.

In Euclid mode the three left-hand knobs change job: Map X, Map Y and Chaos become the pattern lengths of channels 1, 2 and 3 (PhasorBeatMap.cpp:145-147), while the Fill knobs still set the fill. The Acc outputs then carry the point at which each channel's Euclidean pattern wraps rather than an accent (PhasorBeatMapPatternGenerator.cpp:285-295). None of this is in the README.

Chaos has no effect at all until the phasor returns to 0: the bar is redrawn only on a detected phasor reset (PhasorBeatMap.cpp:159-163).

The panel prints only the row and column labels: Phasor, Mode, Map X, Map Y and Chaos down the left, and the columns 1, 2 and 3 crossed with the rows Fill, Trig and Acc. The maker's tooltips name the channels Channel 1 to Channel 3; the original Grids calls them bass drum, snare and hi-hat, which is where the source's BD, SN and HH names come from.

lines: Wavetable oscillator read by a phasor rather than by its own pitch: the input voltage reads straight across one wave of a wavetable loaded from a WAV file
Sweeps through the waves of the loaded wavetable, from the first wave at 0% to the last at 100%, crossfading between neighbouring waves on the way
Scales the Position CV jack below, -100% to +100%, inverting it below 0; at 0 the jack has no effect at all
Unipolar lifts the output by 5V so it runs 0 to 10V; Bipolar leaves it running -5V to +5V
LFO reads the wavetable as it is, with no antialiasing; VCO picks a bandlimited copy of the wave to suit how fast the phasor is moving, which keeps aliasing down at audio rates
A ramp from 0V to 10V reads once straight across the wave; the voltage is divided by 10 and wrapped, so anything outside 0 to 10V comes back round rather than stopping at the end
Added to the Position knob after the trimpot above it scales the voltage, with 10V covering the whole wavetable at a full trimpot; the total is held between the first and last wave
The wave read at the phasor's position, running -5V to +5V, or 0 to 10V with the Offset switch set to Unipolar

Note — a phasor drives this, not a pitch: a ramp rising from 0V to 10V once per cycle, from Phasor Generator, Clock to Phasor or an LFO saw. With nothing patched in, the output holds a steady voltage.
Note — the display shows the name of the loaded wavetable and the wave now being read. A WAV file dropped onto it is loaded straight away; the display itself cannot be clicked for help.
Note — the module comes up with a built-in four-wave table called Basic.wav, holding a sine, a triangle, a sawtooth and a square. A loaded wavetable is saved into the patch and travels with it.
Menu — Mode: LFO (no antialiasing), VCO (antialiased) — the same choice as the Mode switch on the panel
Menu — Initialize wavetable — replaces whatever is loaded with the built-in sine, triangle, sawtooth and square
Menu — Load wavetable — opens a file dialogue for a WAV, AIFF or raw sample file to read as the wavetable
Menu — Save wavetable — writes the loaded wavetable out as a WAV file
Menu — Wave points: 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384 — sets how many samples make up one wave, and so where the loaded file is cut into separate waves

PhasorWavetable.notes:
Read from the repository at commit 56bf82b, the tip of the default branch, whose plugin.json is byte-for-byte the installed one at version 2.0.0.

This module does follow the HetrickCV pattern its sibling breaks: the jacks are read with getPolyVoltage, bounded by the phasor input's channel count, so it is polyphonic to 16 channels, and the phasor wraps rather than clamping.

The output is given no range in the port fields because it has two: the wave is multiplied by 5 after an optional offset of 1 (PhasorWavetable.hpp:586-588), giving -5V to +5V with the switch at Bipolar and 0V to 10V at Unipolar.

The Mode switch and the Mode menu item set the same parameter (PhasorWavetable.cpp:41-43), so the menu item is worth a line: it is the only place the two settings are spelled out in words.

VCO mode measures the phasor's rate of change sample by sample and picks a bandlimited octave of the wavetable from it (PhasorWavetable.hpp:561-578), so a phasor that jumps about will change the brightness of the tone as well as the position in the wave.

When the wavetable is still loading, or the wave is shorter than two points, the output is forced to 0V (PhasorWavetable.hpp:544 and 592-594).

The panel prints Position beside the knob, a minus and a plus either side of the trimpot, VCO and LFO beside the upper switch, Unipolar and Bipolar beside the lower one, and In and Out beside the two jacks.
